blocks.text: The Messages lesson introduced requests as one of three message shapes, this lesson goes deep on requests specifically, the message type that kicks off nearly everything that happens in MCP, discovering tools, calling one, reading a resource, all of it starts with a request.
1. The Four Parts of a Request

blocks.alt: jsonrpc, id, method, and params make up a request

blocks.text: Every request has exactly four parts, a jsonrpc field marking the protocol version, an id uniquely identifying this specific request, a method naming what operation is being asked for, and params, the specific arguments that operation needs.

blocks.title: A quick way to remember them
blocks.content: Version says what language we are speaking, id says which conversation this belongs to, method says what is being asked, params says the specifics.

blocks.text: Every client library abstracts away the raw JSON shown here, but understanding it directly makes debugging a broken integration dramatically easier when something does not behave as expected.

blocks.title: A quick sanity check
blocks.content: If a JSON object is missing an id but has a method, it is a notification, not a request, exactly the distinction covered in the Messages lesson.

blocks.text: Once these four parts feel automatic, reading any MCP related documentation, or debugging a raw network trace, becomes noticeably easier.
2. Method Names Follow a Namespaced Convention

blocks.alt: tools/call and resources/read follow the same naming convention

blocks.text: MCP method names follow a category/action pattern, tools/list, tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get, this namespacing makes it immediately clear which part of the protocol a given method belongs to just by reading its name.
This naming convention also makes documentation and tooling easier to build, a whole category of methods can be described together simply by referencing their shared namespace prefix.
Learning this convention once transfers directly to reading any new MCP server documentation, the method names alone usually tell you most of what you need to know before reading further.
3. The id Field Is the Sender’s Responsibility

Whoever sends a request chooses its id, typically an incrementing counter, the only real requirement is that it be unique enough within the current session to avoid ambiguity when matching the eventual response.
Some implementations use a string id instead of a number, both are valid, JSON-RPC does not mandate one or the other, only that it be usable for exact matching.
A client that restarts mid-session usually starts its id counter fresh, which is fine, since ids only need to be unique within one active session, not across the lifetime of an application.
4. params Shape Depends Entirely on the Method

blocks.alt: A method determines the params shape

blocks.text: There is no single fixed shape for params, a tools/call request needs a tool name and arguments, a resources/read request needs a URI, the method name determines what params are expected, this is exactly why tool schemas and resource URIs matter so much elsewhere in this curriculum.
This is exactly why a client cannot construct a valid tools/call request without first knowing that tool’s inputSchema, discovered ahead of time through tools/list.

code.content:
# a request that would fail schema validation on the server
{"method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"cty": "Mumbai"}}}   # typo, missing required "city"

blocks.text: This is a direct, practical reason why discovery, covered throughout this curriculum, always has to happen before invocation, there is no way to safely guess a method correct params shape without first knowing it.
5. Requests Without params
Not every request needs params at all, tools/list typically needs none, since it is simply asking for the full list of available tools with no further qualification.
Even when a method needs no params, the request is still a complete, valid message, an empty or absent params field is a normal, expected shape, not an error.
Whether a specific method requires params is part of what the protocol specification, or the server documentation, defines for that method, not something a client should have to guess.
6. Every Request Expects Exactly One Response

blocks.alt: One request expects exactly one response

blocks.text: A request is always answered with exactly one response, never zero and never more than one, if a server cannot fulfill the request for any reason, it still must send back a response, just one containing an error rather than a result.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: A client relying on a strict one-to-one mapping between requests and responses would break immediately if a server ever sent back two responses to the same request, or none at all.

blocks.text: This one-to-one guarantee is also what makes it safe for a client to track pending requests in a simple lookup table, confident each entry will be resolved exactly once.

If a client ever does receive an unexpected second response for the same id, the safest behavior is to log it as an anomaly and ignore the duplicate, rather than trying to reconcile two conflicting results.
7. Requests Can Be Sent Concurrently

blocks.alt: Request A and request B can be sent concurrently

blocks.text: A client is not required to wait for one request’s response before sending the next, several requests can be in flight simultaneously, each tracked independently by its own id, until its matching response arrives.

code.content:
id_a = client.send_request("tools/list")
id_b = client.send_request("resources/list")
# both may be in flight at once, responses matched back by id when they arrive

blocks.text: This concurrency is especially useful when a client needs information from several independent sources at once, listing tools and listing resources at the same time rather than waiting for one before starting the other.

blocks.title: A practical limit
blocks.content: Even though concurrency is allowed, a well-behaved client usually still caps how many requests it keeps in flight at once, to avoid overwhelming a server or itself.

blocks.text: This is one of the reasons a well-designed host feels responsive even when several pieces of information need to be gathered at once, waiting on the slowest of several parallel requests rather than the sum of all of them run one after another.
8. The Initialize Request Is Special

blocks.alt: The initialize request must come first

blocks.text: The very first request of any session is always the initialize request, announcing the client’s supported capabilities and protocol version, no other request is valid until this one has been sent and answered.
Sending any other request before initialize completes is considered a protocol violation, well-behaved servers will reject it, reinforcing just how foundational this first handshake really is.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Request order","Valid"],"rows":[["initialize first","Yes"],["tools/list before initialize","No, protocol violation"]]}

blocks.text: This first request is also where the client reveals its own supported protocol version, giving the server a chance to reject the connection early if the versions are fundamentally incompatible.
9. Cancelling a Request

blocks.alt: An in-flight request gets cancelled and stopped

blocks.text: Some implementations support cancelling a request that is still in flight, useful for a long-running tool call the user no longer wants to wait for, this is typically done by sending a separate notification referencing the original request’s id.

code.content:
# a cancellation notification referencing the original request id
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/cancelled", "params": {"requestId": 7}}

blocks.text: Not every operation can be meaningfully cancelled once started, a server should document clearly which of its tools support cancellation and which do not.

blocks.title: A practical use case
blocks.content: A user closing a chat window mid-request is a natural moment to send a cancellation, freeing up server resources that would otherwise keep working on a result nobody will see.

blocks.text: A server that ignores a cancellation and completes the work anyway is not necessarily wrong, but it should still avoid sending a result the client never asked to receive after cancelling.
10. Requests and Timeouts

A client should not wait forever for a response, a sensible timeout, covered in full in the Timeouts lesson in the Transport Mechanisms module, protects against a request that will simply never be answered due to a dropped connection or an unresponsive server.

blocks.title: A reasonable default
blocks.content: Many client implementations use a timeout somewhere between a few seconds and a minute by default, adjusted upward for tools known to be slow, like generating a long report.

blocks.text: Choosing too short a timeout risks prematurely giving up on a slow but otherwise healthy request, choosing too long a timeout risks a poor user experience when something has genuinely gone wrong.
11. Requests From Server to Client

Most requests flow from client to server, but the protocol does allow a server to send a request back to the client in some cases, for example, asking the client to confirm a risky action before proceeding, this reversed direction still follows the exact same request shape.
This reversed direction is uncommon in simple servers, but becomes more relevant in advanced patterns like human-in-the-loop confirmation, covered later in this curriculum.
12. Logging Requests for Debugging

Logging every outgoing request, including its full method name and params, is one of the simplest and most effective habits for debugging an MCP-based system, when something goes wrong, the request log usually shows exactly what was actually asked for.
Pairing this with response logging, covered in the next lesson, gives a complete picture, exactly what was asked for and exactly what came back, side by side.
Structured logging, keeping method, id, and params as separate searchable fields rather than one giant string, makes it far easier to filter and analyze request logs at scale.
13. A Worked Example
Trace constructing a request from scratch for calling a specific tool, including choosing an id and shaping the params correctly.
Notice the helper function only adds params when they are actually provided, correctly producing the simpler, params-free shape for a method like tools/list that needs none.

Try extending this helper function to also validate that arguments matches the target tool’s inputSchema before the request is even sent, catching a mistake earlier rather than waiting for a server-side rejection.
14. Common Mistakes When Working With Requests

items: Reusing the same id for two different in-flight requests, breaking the client’s ability to match responses correctly.
Sending a request before the initialize handshake has completed, before the session is actually ready.
Assuming every request needs params, some, like tools/list, typically need none at all.
Never setting a timeout, and waiting indefinitely on a request that will never receive a response.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is forgetting that request-response pairing depends entirely on the id, not on the order messages happen to arrive in.
A sixth common mistake is not handling the case where a response never arrives at all, due to a dropped connection, without a timeout in place, a client can hang indefinitely.
15. Practice: Construct Your Own Requests
Write out, by hand, the exact JSON for a resources/read request for a specific file URI, and for a prompts/get request filling in a specific prompt’s arguments.
Once you have written both requests by hand, try writing the corresponding response you would expect back for each one, reinforcing the connection covered in the next lesson.
As a final step, deliberately introduce a mistake into one of your hand-written requests, like a missing required argument, and predict what error response you would expect back.
Key Takeaway

A request is a jsonrpc-versioned, uniquely identified message naming a specific method and, usually, params shaped to match that method, every meaningful operation in MCP starts as a request, expects exactly one response, and can be sent concurrently with others as long as ids stay unique.
This lesson builds directly on the brief introduction from the Messages lesson, and connects forward to Responses next, the other half of every request-response exchange.
The request-from-server concept covered in the newly added section is a good reminder that MCP’s message shapes are symmetric, the same request format works regardless of which side initiates it.
